answers.question: My club mate runs 70 miles a week before a marathon. I'm thinking of doubling to 80 next week to catch up, running twice a day. Would that work?
answers.answer:
No. Doubling from 40 to 80 miles in one week, with doubles you have never run, is the fastest way to get hurt five weeks before the race. Safe building adds roughly 10 percent at a time, and you started this build at about 30 miles a week.

You have already seen what a big jump costs. After the 53-mile week your calves were tight, and your legs still felt heavy early this week. An 80-mile week would cost far more, just when your biggest long runs are due.

The timing also works against you. A week of training takes two to three weeks to show up as fitness. An 80-mile week now would show up as fatigue during your peak and taper.

Your club mate's 70 miles took months or years to build. What counts is the load you can absorb, and this load is working. Your easy heart rate is steady at 139, and you held marathon pace for 6 miles on Wednesday.

Doubles are also the wrong tool for a marathon. Two short runs add fatigue without the long, unbroken time on your feet that the race demands.

Here is what you can do instead. Run 45 miles next week and the high 40s the week after, with the extra going into a 9-mile Thursday and a longer Sunday. That is a real increase, and you will still be fresh enough to race well.

new.analysis:
**You ran this week exactly as planned.** Every run matched its planned distance, pain stayed at 0/10, and both rest days were real rest. After the 53-mile week that was the right call, and the heavy legs had cleared by Thursday.

**Wednesday's run shows 3:45 is realistic, but with little to spare.** Your 6 marathon-pace miles averaged about 8:36/mi, right on the 8:35/mi that 3:45 needs. Heart rate climbed to 160 and it felt like effort 7/10, so you can hold the pace, but it is not yet comfortable.

**Your easy share of 64 percent is below the 80 percent target, but it is not a worry.** Your easy runs stayed almost entirely in zone 2. The rest came from the marathon-pace block, which belongs in zone 3, and from Sunday's long run, which averaged 146 bpm with 55 percent in zone 3.

**Your mileage has climbed quickly since late August, so next week adds only 5 miles.** The 53-mile week was a one-off spike, and next week builds from the 40 you just absorbed.

| Week | Miles | Long run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aug 17 – 23 | 24 | 10 mi |
| Aug 24 – 30 | 27 | 11 mi |
| Aug 31 – Sep 6 | 37 | 14 mi |
| Sep 7 – 13 | 53 | 20 mi |
| Sep 14 – 20 | 40 | 15 mi |
| Sep 21 – 27 (planned) | 45 | 17 mi |

**The extra miles go where they help the marathon most.** A 9-mile Thursday gives you a second longer run during the week, which builds endurance without adding another hard day. The two harder sessions are Wednesday's threshold reps and Sunday's race-pace finish, with easy days and rest between them.

**The long run goes to 17 miles, not 20, because of what it now includes.** You ran 20 miles two weeks ago, so distance is not what you are missing. Four race-pace miles late in the run are more specific work than three more easy miles would be.

**Keep your two strength sessions, but not on Saturday.** That way Sunday's race-pace miles start on fresh legs.

**The next two weeks are your peak, then the taper starts Oct 12.** Sep 28 – Oct 4 and Oct 5 – 11 will hold one more 20-miler and more marathon-pace work. After that, volume drops toward race day on Sun Nov 1.
